title: The True Meaning of Practice
excerpt: The mind is like a continuously flowing river. If you cannot use your practice to grasp it in every present moment, then the mantras you recite, the visualizations you do, the chanting, the meditation, and even the lofty views you express and the exalted conduct you display — all of this is merely wasting time.

inline.s: Dilgo Khyentse Rinpoche
The mind
is like a continuously flowing river
If you cannot use your practice

to grasp it in every present moment, then the mantras you recite, the visualizations you do, the chanting, the meditation, and even the lofty views you express and the exalted conduct you display — all of this is merely wasting time.
The essence of practice holds nothing at all strange; its substance is simply to repeatedly go deep into our mental continuum and to transform it; otherwise, this precious human body will be wasted
You spend a whole lifetime chasing your own thoughts, clinging to the samsara they create, and in truth you are losing yourself within a dream without ever realizing it.
Start each day from the small and subtle things; do not expect wondrous splendor. See through these tricks of vanity and observe your own mind closely
Even if in this very life you cannot completely transform your mind, and even if you cannot make great progress in realization, as long as you carefully guard your three deeds
(bodily, verbal, and mental deeds)
, and look
after
each of your own thoughts

Though you cannot attain even waking within sleep, or control your mind even in serious illness, as long as you diligently work on each of your thoughts, diligently and devoutly tending your own deepest inner being rather than merely putting on an outward show, then — as Chökyi Wangpo sang in the Auspicious King, the Essence of the Three Essentials of the Great Perfection: “Even if you do not attain in this life, the mind is still at peace, truly joyful.” Why? On the inner level, you have transformed your mind, and thereby transformed your life: peace, compassion, and letting go have already shown forth the greatest accomplishment.
Accomplishment is divided into outer, inner, secret, and most secret:
First, at the level of outer accomplishment, this is intellectual accomplishment
Though you have mastered great knowledge and understood profound views,
yet

unfortunately, they are like patches sewn onto a garment, and in the end they will fall away. For example, when we are healthy we feel very much at ease, and since we have this knowledge of the Dharma, all of it hints, with a pleasing sense of self, that we seem to be extraordinary sages

But when you meet with serious illness and, burning all over, sink into unconsciousness, look closely at your mind: it is utterly beyond your control, and all kinds of karmic signs nearing death display themselves in dreams. Even though you loathe them and dare not fall into the murk of sleep, unconsciousness soon overwhelms you

At that time, all your intelligence and learning are of no avail to you. So the practitioner should know that when ordinary and even terrifying dreams continue unabated in serious illness, this is a disgrace to one's practice — indeed a disgrace to one's study and reflection. To have never put it into practice, or to practice only on the surface, is like the mist on a mirror: it does not last long.
Secondly
at the level of inner accomplishment, this is the accomplishment of meditative experience
When joy and light arise, and great stillness is accompanied by deep bliss, and you can even see all sorts of strange visions, and
are able
to know events beforehand
These experiences are like shouting at a great mountain valley: you cry out with effort and it throws back at you a mighty echo, yet in a moment it is gone. If you strive
to practice
with diligence, then all sorts of strange experiences will arise; but remember, everything in this world is subject to impermanence
If you wish to have these experiences and possess them forever, then you will suffer like one who tries to catch the moon
in
the water — they are essentially impermanent. So free yourself from all the fantasies of meditative experience!
Do not try to possess them; look upon them with perfect
equanimity,
without disturbing the mind's inner continuum
Even if, within a vast state of even-minded realization, everything manifests as unreal mists of five colors or rainbow light, and you are able with great ease
to
pass through walls

or press your handprint into rock, yet to regard these as marks of enlightenment and to give rise to pride is the beginning of coming under the spell of a demon, and, because of self-clinging, to wandering in samsara.
Lastly
at the level of secret and most secret accomplishment, this is the vast accomplishment of primordial wisdom
This means we
treat life with equanimity and, at ease,
abide in the vast nature of mind, where everything becomes the majestic natural liberation
and
dispelled

In the wisdom of one's own mind, clinging and afflictions have been dissolved; compassionate and vast-hearted, one is such that nothing in life can disturb this inner wisdom of which nothing remains, transcending joy and sorrow and resting naturally in the present moment.
Through the practice of the mind, we pass through various different stages
In the end, our mind becomes a single taste of emptiness and luminosity; neither fear nor hope can occupy the mind — this is the way of the Buddha.
